title: The Bhagats close
hook: the Guru's book is a house with room for saints of every kind

segments.voice: Yesterday, one Guru: the bani is the Guru, and your line, one bow covers them all. Today, the Bhagats' block closes.

A big family dinner, and the extra chairs keep coming out of the back room. A cousin's new husband. A neighbor nobody expected. The aunt who isn't speaking to the uncle, seated three chairs away from him. Somehow the table stretches, and nobody is sent home to eat alone. For a long stretch now, you and i have been walking through a book that works like that table. Today the question is simple: who got a chair?
screen: `A LONG FAMILY TABLE.` → `MORE CHAIRS FROM THE BACK.` → `WHO GOT A CHAIR?`

segments.voice: Look down the table. Kabir, the weaver of Benares, with his warp and weft and his sharp tongue. Sheikh Farid of Pakpattan, a Sufi, asking you to look under your own collar. Namdev, the calico printer, whose temple, tradition says, turned to face him. Ravidas, the shoemaker, whose family carried the dead cattle, dreaming of Begampura. Then the others. Trilochan and the last thought. Beni and the stages of life. Dhanna the farmer. Sain the barber. Pipa the king. Sadhna's plea for grace. Ramanand's home colored with love. Parmanand: hear, then do. Surdas's single line. Jaidev, the old poet. Bhikhan's medicine. And around them, the Bhatts with their praise, Satta and Balvand forgiven and sung, the saloks to Mardana, Sundar's call. A weaver beside a king. A Muslim saint beside a Hindu devotee. A man from a family others kept at a distance beside a Brahmin. Guru Arjan, in Raag Suhi on Ang 747, says in paraphrase that the teaching is shared by all four castes, the Khatri, the Brahmin, the Shudra and the Vaishya alike. The Bhagat pages put that line into practice: the Gurus didn't just say the table was open, they set the places. And the room wasn't made by agreeing on everything. The Gurus kept voices they answered, sometimes putting the same image another way. The table holds difference without throwing anyone out. Tomorrow the path turns from the book to the people around the Gurus, starting at home, with Guru Nanak's mother and father.
screen: `WEAVER, SUFI, CALICO PRINTER, SHOEMAKER.` · `FARMER, BARBER, KING, AND MORE.` · `ONE TEACHING FOR ALL FOUR CASTES.` · `ROOM WITHOUT AGREEING ON EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `ROOM FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who usually ends up on the edge: of a conversation, a group chat, a family gathering. Don't fix anything; just picture a chair being pulled out for them at your table, and breathe with that picture, with Waheguru on each breath out if you pray.
Sant. A saint or holy person: the weaver, the Sufi, the shoemaker, the farmer, the barber and the king, all honored this way at one table.
Your line: room for all. The table stretches, and nobody eats alone. That's day eight hundred one.

howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing the Bhagats' hymns as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs point to them, along with langar and the shared sangat, as the Guru's teaching that the door is open to people of every caste and faith.

chat.says: Why does the Sikh scripture include hymns by Muslim and Hindu saints?
options: The Gurus opened the table to every caste and background, even voices they answered.
Those saints were secretly Sikhs, so their hymns were simply counted as Sikh hymns.
Scribes added them much later; the Gurus themselves never chose those hymns.
chat.meaning: Guru Arjan sings that the teaching is shared by all four castes; the Bhagat pages put that into practice, difference and all.

Pakpattan.meaning: Sheikh Farid's town in the Punjab

Khatri.meaning: one of the four castes Guru Arjan names
